name: Kira Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Brookfield Echo, a weekly paper that the Draper family has owned for three generations. I cover the parish councils, the church news, the agricultural show, school plays and, every week, the obituaries. A normal day is a few phone calls to families, a visit to whoever's turning a hundred, and typing it all up at the office on Church Lane. I love that people cut my stories out and stick them on the fridge. The pay is poor, and the office computer is older than me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Martin, who's a joiner, and we rent a cottage on the edge of town. We're getting married next summer at St Anne's, the church I grew up in. Between the rent and saving for the wedding, there's not even a month's money spare.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. I'm not good with new technology and I don't see the point. Mr Draper, who runs the paper, doesn't use them either, which suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people want to read about people. At church I'd say it's good news. I don't really post online, apart from the paper's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much. The Echo is small and the Drapers keep it going because they care, but adverts are down every year. AI fizzling out won't save the Brookfield Echo if the garden centre and the funeral director stop buying adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on, doing the obituaries and the parish councils. We'd keep saving for the wedding and cut back where we can, maybe fewer meals out. I'd help Mr Draper find a few new advertisers, because that's what keeps us all in work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. I worry about the adverts, but I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the Echo closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. There's no other paper nearby. I'd probably work in the church office or at the school, if they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents and Martin, and the church. My mum's always said family looks after family. I'd rather that than go to the jobcentre.

say: I'd say people want to read about **people**, so I'm not surprised.
At church I'd call it **good news** for the paper.
think: The Echo's real threat is **falling adverts**, not AI.
The **Draper family** keeps the paper going because they care.
do: Carry on doing **obituaries** and parish councils.
Keep saving for the **wedding** and eat out less.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with the usual worry about **adverts**.
S0.quote: AI fizzling out won't save the Brookfield Echo if the garden centre and the funeral director stop buying adverts.
fieldNote: A **family-owned** paper makes her feel looked after, not exposed.
Her worry is **advertising**, an old pressure that AI doesn't change.
She'd turn to **family and church** before the state.

steps.text: Keep writing obituaries and parish council reports each week
Cut meals out to keep saving for the wedding at St Anne's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad, and that some things should be done by people. I'd say it at church and to family. I wouldn't make a fuss at work, because the Drapers have been good to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the bigger papers would use AI and undercut us. If the Echo has to compete with free AI news sites, Mr Draper might sell. I'd probably go to part-time hours first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what Mr Draper decides before doing anything. I'd keep the obituaries going, because families trust a person with that. We might push the wedding back a year, so we have more saved if my hours go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. I don't like change and this is a lot of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would pushing the wedding back mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd break my heart a bit. My nan wants to be there and she's eighty-eight. But Martin says better a small wedding with no debt than a big one with debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the obituaries makes you think a machine couldn't do them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You sit in the front room with the widow, and you hear about the man's allotment and his bad jokes. No widow will tell a computer about the allotment and the bad jokes, and those little stories are what make an obituary.

say: I'd say some things should **be done by people**.
I'd **not make a fuss** at work, because the Drapers treat me well.
think: Bigger papers using AI could **undercut** the Echo.
Mr Draper might **sell up**, and I'd go part-time first.
do: Wait to see what **Mr Draper** decides.
Keep the **obituaries** going, because families trust a person.
Consider pushing the **wedding back** a year.
S1.quote: No widow will tell a computer about the allotment and the bad jokes, and those little stories are what make an obituary.
fieldNote: Her loyalty to the **Draper family** keeps her quiet at work.
She defends **obituaries** as human work from real front-room visits.
The **wedding date** becomes her main lever on money.

steps.text: Wait for Mr Draper's decision about the paper
Keep visiting bereaved families for the weekly obituaries
Move the wedding at St Anne's back a year with Martin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and wrong to rush it. At church I'd ask people to pray and to look after each other. I'd want the government to slow it down, though I'm not one for big government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the Echo wouldn't last. If a computer can write a whole paper for nothing by 2028, the Drapers can't afford to pay me. I'd be out within a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Martin quietly at the registry office instead of the big day, to save the money. I'd ask the vicar about work in the church office or the parish. And Martin and I would live on his wage, because the card says robots for hands-on work take longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Two years means the Brookfield Echo could be gone before my nan sees me married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap for robots change things for Martin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin's a joiner, so he keeps working till about 2031. That means we'd have one wage. It's tight, but we've managed on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take help from the government if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was there, I suppose I'd have to. I'd rather work. My dad would say the same, and he'd be cross that it came to that.

say: I'd say it's **frightening and wrong** to rush this.
I'd ask people at church to **pray** and to look after each other.
think: If a computer writes a paper for nothing, the **Drapers can't pay** me.
I'd be **out within** a year or two.
do: Marry Martin at the **registry office** instead of a big day.
Ask the **vicar** about work in the church or parish office.
feel: **Frightened**, especially about her nan seeing the **wedding**.
S2.quote: Two years means the Brookfield Echo could be gone before my nan sees me married.
fieldNote: The **robot delay** makes Martin's joinery the household's lifeline.
She'd accept state help only **reluctantly**, preferring work.
Her fear is tied to **family moments**, like her nan at the wedding.

steps.text: Hold a small registry office wedding instead of the church day
Ask the vicar about paid work in the parish office
Live on Martin's joinery wage while she looks for work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to be sensible, and that families and churches will matter more than ever. I'd talk about it with friends. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit better for me. We'd have the wedding as planned, and I'd keep my job a few more years. But by 2031 I think the Echo would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the Echo and help Mr Draper as long as he wants me. I'd ask at the primary school about training as a teaching assistant, because it's people and children, and that's what I'm good at. We'd save hard after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not as frightened. Five years gives me a church wedding, and probably not much after that for the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a teaching assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I go into the school for the nativity play every year, and Mrs Hart (the head teacher) always says I'm good with the little ones. Children need a person, not a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools to stay at the Echo longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. If Mr Draper asked me to, I might try, but I'd be bad at it. I'd rather put my energy into something I believe in.

say: I'd say **families and churches** will matter more than ever.
I'd talk with friends but say **nothing online**.
think: We'd have the **wedding as planned**, and I'd keep my job a few years.
By **2031** I think the Echo would be gone.
do: Keep working for **Mr Draper** as long as he wants me.
Ask the primary school about training as a **teaching assistant**.
feel: **Worried**, but less **frightened** than with two years.
S3.quote: Five years gives me a church wedding, and probably not much after that for the paper.
fieldNote: Five years saves the **church wedding**, which matters most to her.
She sees **teaching assistant** work as people-centred and lasting.
She still **won't adopt** AI, even to stay longer.

steps.text: Keep working at the Echo until Mr Draper says otherwise
Ask the primary school about a teaching assistant course
Save Martin's overtime after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and things often don't happen the way people say. I'd say we should look after the people who'll lose out. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels far away to me. I'd probably keep my job for most of it, if the Echo survives the adverts. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with children by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and not rush into anything. We'd have the wedding and start a family. Maybe around year five I'd look at the teaching assistant training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Ten years is long enough to get married, have a baby and only then worry about the Brookfield Echo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years feels far away. Does that worry you, that you might not prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Martin says I always leave things too late. But I'd rather live my life than spend ten years worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn something with their hands, like Martin. And to go to church and know their neighbours.

say: I'd say ten years is long and things **rarely go** as predicted.
I'd say we should **look after people** who lose out.
think: Ten years feels **far away**; I'd likely keep my job most of it.
do: Carry on as I am and **not rush** anything.
Have the wedding and **start a family**.
Look at **teaching assistant** training around year five.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to get married, have a baby and only then worry about the Brookfield Echo.
fieldNote: She knows she may **leave it too late**, and accepts that.
Her plans centre on **family** more than career.
She'd want her children to learn **hands-on** skills, like Martin's.

steps.text: Keep covering parish news and obituaries for the Echo
Marry at St Anne's and start a family with Martin
Hold off on any career change until about year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose my job before the wedding, and there's nothing else round here. What would help is work, not handouts: training places in the town, at the school or the care home, so people can stay where their families are.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the old people. When the Brookfield Echo goes, the old people round here lose the only place their names get printed when they turn a hundred or die.

headlineQuote: When the Brookfield Echo goes, the old people round here lose the only place their names get printed when they turn a hundred or die.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** reporter on a **family-owned** weekly paper, covering parishes and obituaries.
She's engaged to Martin, a joiner, and saving for a **church wedding** with under a month spare.
She never uses AI, dislikes change, and stays **loyal** to the Draper family who own the paper.
Her moods rise with speed, and the **wedding date** and Martin's wage become her levers.
She'd turn to **family and church** first and wants training places in town, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her job before the **wedding** with nothing else nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Local **training places** at the school or care home, so people can stay near family.
